name: Jamal Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, that's fine. I'm not much of a talker about this stuff, but I'll be honest with you. Just don't put my agency's name anywhere.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at seven with Mr Okafor, who had a stroke last year, so it's getting him up, washed, dressed and his tablets out of the blister pack. Then it's twelve or thirteen more calls, most of them fifteen or thirty minutes, all over the east side of the city on two buses. We only get paid for the time inside the house, not the bus, so a long day is eleven hours for maybe eight hours' pay. The bit I like is the people, honestly, like Mrs Lindqvist who sings old songs while I do her stockings. The bit that wears me out is the phone app that clocks us in and out, and the care notes, because I'm slow at typing and I left school at fifteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hype, yeah, that's what I've been saying. Nobody's sending a computer to put Mr Okafor's socks on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say in the break room at the depot: told you so. Care is people, and you can't fake people. Maybe I'd post something on the union group chat about how they should spend the money on carers instead of gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means nothing gets better either. I'm still on the same pay, still not paid for the bus, still doing split shifts that wreck my evenings with Noor, my girlfriend. AI flopping doesn't fix any of the stuff that's actually wrong with this job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, carry on like now. I'd keep paying my union subs, keep my three months of savings where they are, and push the union rep about getting travel time paid. Maybe finally finish the care certificate modules I keep putting off, because the manager keeps asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, a bit. But tired too, because the normal version of this job is already hard. It's not a scary picture, it's just the same grind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nothing gets better either. What's the thing you'd most want fixed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid travel time, no question. Last month Bev, an older carer on my patch, got docked because the app said she left a client four minutes early, and she'd only gone to fetch a towel from the line. That's why I joined the union. If AI doesn't come, those fights are still the fights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the money go now, with three months saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent first, then the bus pass, then food. Noor works at the bakery counter in the big supermarket, so between us we cover it, just. The savings is for if one of us gets sick, because my agency doesn't pay proper sick pay. A bad winter with flu could eat half of it.

say: AI flopping proves **care is people**, and you can't fake that with a gadget.
The money should go to **carers' wages**, not to tech the bosses don't need.
think: Nothing improves either: I'm still on **unpaid travel** and split shifts that wreck my evenings.
A **bad winter** with flu and no proper sick pay could eat half my savings.
do: Keep paying **union subs** and push the rep to get travel time paid this year.
Finish the **care certificate** modules the manager keeps chasing him about.
Leave the **three months saved** untouched as a sick-pay buffer.
feel: **Relieved** that robots aren't coming, but **tired** of a grind that stays the same.
S0.quote: AI flopping doesn't fix any of the stuff that's actually wrong with this job.
fieldNote: His worries are about **pay and conditions**, not technology, so the plateau barely moves him.
A colleague docked by the **tracking app** is what pushed him into the union.
Savings are seen as a **sick-pay substitute**, because the agency doesn't cover illness properly.

steps.text: Push the union rep for paid travel time between calls
Finish the outstanding care certificate modules before spring
Keep three months' rent untouched for sick weeks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking tasks, so the office stuff. That's not me, mostly, but I bet they'd use it on us somehow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say: watch, they'll use it to squeeze us. Online I'd share the union's posts about it. I'd say AI should do the paperwork so we get more time with clients, not so they can cut the visits shorter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, my job's safe for now. A computer can't lift an old woman onto the commode. Software doesn't care that I need ten minutes between streets either. The office girls who do the rota now, Priya and Dawn, they'd be out of a job, and they're the ones who swap shifts for us when someone's sick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union to get it in writing that no AI rota can book calls back to back with no travel. I'd let the app do my care notes by voice if they made me, because typing is the bit I'm worst at, but I wouldn't go looking for it. I'd keep saving what I can, maybe twenty a week more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Annoyed more than scared. It's like the tracking app all over again, something new watching me. But my hands are still needed, so I can sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use voice notes if they made you. Would that actually help you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, yeah, I'll admit it. I spend twenty minutes every evening on the bus typing notes with one thumb and getting told off for spelling. If I could just say 'Mr Okafor ate half his porridge, skin's fine on his heel' and it wrote it up, that'd be better. I just don't trust who reads it after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya in the office, she's a single mum and she does the rota. If the software does her job, she's gone, and nobody'll know the clients like she does. She knows which old man won't open the door to a new face.

say: They'll use AI to **squeeze carers**, not to give us more time with clients.
AI should take the **paperwork**, and the visit time should stay with the person.
think: A computer can't lift a client, so **my hands** are still needed for now.
Software doing the **rota** means no slack between streets and the office staff gone.
do: Ask the **union** to win a written rule against back-to-back calls with no travel.
Use **voice notes** for care records only if the agency requires it.
Save about **twenty a week** more than now.
feel: **Annoyed**, like the tracking app all over again, but not losing sleep.
S1.quote: A computer can't lift an old woman onto the commode. Software doesn't care that I need ten minutes between streets either.
fieldNote: He separates his **hands-on work**, which he sees as safe, from the office jobs he expects to go.
Admits **voice notes** would help with typing, which is his weakest skill.
His concern is for the **rota coordinator**, a single mum, more than for himself.

steps.text: Ask the union for a written ban on no-travel rotas
Use voice-to-text care notes only if the agency requires it
Put twenty a week more into the savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's mad. And robots doing hands-on stuff by 2031, so that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd be saying the government has to step in, because care is the last thing you hand to a machine. Online I'd be angry, I'll be honest, sharing every petition. I'd say the people who built this never wiped anyone's bottom in their life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I've got about five years and then I'm done. By 2028 the office and the rota and the care plans are all AI, and by 2031 there's a robot that can hoist and wash and do tablets. The council pays the agency per hour, and if a robot is cheaper per hour, the council takes the robot. I've got no qualifications to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd go to every union meeting and get Noor to sign the petitions too. I'd stop the little spends, like the takeaway on Fridays, and try to get the savings up to six months by 2030. I'd finally finish my care certificate, because at least then I'm the qualified one they keep longest. I don't know what else, honestly, I'm not a computer person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. I'd be lying awake thinking about it. I'd be 31 with nothing else on my CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not a computer person. Would you try to learn any of it in those first two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to say yes, but I know myself. I tried an online course once and gave up after the second video. Maybe if the union ran something in a room with a real teacher, I'd go. I'm not doing it on my phone at midnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Between 2028 and 2031, while the robots aren't here yet, what does your job look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably worse. The AI plans every minute of my day and tells me what to do in each house, like a sat nav for washing people. I'd still be the hands, but with no say. Then one day a letter comes saying the robots start in March.

say: Care is the **last thing** you hand to a machine, so the government must step in.
The people who built this **never cared** for anyone, and I'd share every petition.
think: I'd have **about five years** before robots can hoist, wash and do tablets.
The council pays **per hour**, and if a robot is cheaper it takes the robot.
I've got **no qualifications** to fall back on if the job goes.
do: Go to every **union meeting** and get his partner to sign petitions too.
Cut **Friday takeaways** and aim for six months' savings by 2030.
Finish the **care certificate** so he's among the last carers kept.
feel: **Sick** and lying awake, picturing himself at 31 with nothing else on his CV.
S2.quote: The council pays the agency per hour, and if a robot is cheaper per hour, the council takes the robot.
fieldNote: He maps the **two-step timeline** clearly: office work goes in 2028, his hands-on work around 2031.
Wants to learn but expects to **give up** on anything done alone on a phone.
Expects the gap years to make the job **more controlled**, like a sat nav for washing people.
The fear is **no fallback**: he left school at fifteen and has only this job.

steps.text: Attend every union meeting and gather petition signatures
Drop Friday takeaways to reach six months' savings by 2030
Finish the care certificate within the first year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, then robots around 2034. Better than two. I'd be 35.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, I'd say it publicly, care shouldn't be done by machines and the government needs a plan for people like me. But I'd say it calmer, because there'd be time for the union to actually win something, like a rule that a human has to be in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it means I've got until my mid-thirties in this job, and then I don't know. With five years, maybe families push back, because a lot of old people won't let a stranger in, never mind a robot. Mrs Lindqvist screamed at a new carer last month. But the council will go for cheap in the end, I believe that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the certificate this year and maybe do the medication module, since that's the bit they might keep a human for longest. I'd get on the union branch committee instead of just turning up. I'd try to save something every month and not touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not like the two-year one. More like a knot that's always there. I'd still have time to fight it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the council will go for cheap in the end. Then why fight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if we don't, it'll be worse and faster. When they brought in the tracking app, the union got the grace minutes added because we kicked up a fuss. Small wins matter when you're on this pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Noor about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Noor we shouldn't sign for a bigger flat yet, not till we see which way it goes. She'd say I'm being gloomy. She's probably right, but I'd rather be gloomy with savings.

say: Care shouldn't be done by machines, and the government needs a **plan for carers**.
With five years, the union could win a rule that **a human** stays in the room.
think: I've got until my **mid-thirties** in this job, and after that I don't know.
Some **families will refuse** robots, but the council will choose cheap in the end.
do: Finish the certificate and add the **medication module** this year.
Join the **branch committee** instead of only turning up to meetings.
Hold off on a **bigger flat** with his partner until things are clearer.
feel: A **steady knot** of worry, but with time to fight it.
S3.quote: A lot of old people won't let a stranger in, never mind a robot.
fieldNote: Five years turns his response from protest into **steady organising** on the branch committee.
He picks the **medication module** because he guesses humans keep that task longest.
Still expects the **council to buy cheap**, so the fight is about slowing it down.

steps.text: Add the medication module to his care certificate this year
Stand for the union branch committee
Put off a bigger flat with his partner for now
Save a fixed sum every month and leave it alone

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2039 for the robots. I'd be about 40. That's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say what everyone says, that it's ages away and we'll see. At union meetings I'd say we should start pushing for rules now while it's still far off. Online, I'd likely not bother much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years is a long time and I can't think that far. I'll deal with it then. If I'm still a carer at 40 and a robot turns up, at least I'll have had a decade of work and maybe Noor and me will have kids by then and a bit put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now, mostly. Finish the certificate, keep the union stuff going, keep the savings. Maybe in five years I'd look at something like being a senior carer who trains the new ones, because whoever teaches the robots might still need someone who knows the clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. Easy to put to the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd deal with it then. If someone offered you a retraining course now, paid for, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was in a room and they paid me for the hours, yeah, probably. If it's on a website, no. That's just how I am, I'll be honest with you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you take it seriously sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw a robot actually doing a wash on somebody, for real, on the news. Until then it's talk. I've heard bosses promise new tech for years and we still get paper blister packs.

say: It's **ages away**, so we'll see, but the union should push for rules now.
Online, I'd **hardly bother** posting about something ten years off.
think: Ten years is too far ahead to plan, so I'll **deal with it then**.
A decade of work means **savings** and maybe kids before any robot arrives.
do: Keep the **certificate**, union work and savings going as now.
Consider a **senior carer** role training new staff in about five years.
Take **retraining** only if it's in a room and paid.
feel: **Mostly fine**, and easy to push to the back of his mind.
S4.quote: I've heard bosses promise new tech for years and we still get paper blister packs.
fieldNote: A decade lets him **push it away**; he admits he can't plan that far.
He'd only believe it after seeing a **robot do a wash** for real.
Retraining must be **in person and paid**, never on a phone at night.

steps.text: Keep up union work and the monthly savings habit
Wait to see a robot actually washing someone before acting
Look at a senior carer training role in about five years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. Two years for the office stuff and five for my hands isn't enough for someone like me with no qualifications. What would help is the union winning a rule that a human has to do personal care, and a retraining course in a real room where they pay you for the hours, not some app.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Yeah, you didn't ask about the old people. Everyone talks about us carers losing jobs. Mrs Lindqvist is a good example. Nobody asks the old women I look after if they want a robot doing their stockings, and they're the ones it happens to.

headlineQuote: Nobody asks the old women I look after if they want a robot doing their stockings, and they're the ones it happens to.
portrait: A 27-year-old **home care worker** on city bus routes, paid only for time inside clients' homes.
Left school at fifteen, slow at typing, and still **finishing his care certificate**.
Strongly **pro-union**; joined after a colleague was docked by the tracking app.
Sees AI Plateau and Steady Disruption as **same old grind**, with office staff hit first.
Feels **alarmed** by AGI by 2028 but pushes AGI by 2036 to the back of his mind.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years for office work and five for his hands is too little.
whatWouldHelp: A **union rule** that humans do personal care.
**Paid retraining** in a real classroom, not on an app.
